verdict.reasoning: Patient reports skin is ‘sore and red’ and ‘very itchy and, uh, dry, all over my body’ and that it is getting ‘way worse’ over the past few days.

Patient: ‘over the past few days I’ve noticed my skin is sore and red… all over my chest, my hands and arms’ and later ‘It’s very itchy and, uh, dry, all over my body,’ consistent with a few days of widespread pruritic, dry erythema.
Patient: ‘inside of the elbows… Which is the, the worst area,’ corresponding to antecubital fossae being worst.
Patient: ‘It’s very itchy’ and when discussing weeping says ‘but, but, not the areas that are cracked,’ indicating the skin is very itchy and has cracks.

For weeping: Doctor asks if it is weeping and patient replies ‘No. No.’; for excoriations: Doctor asks about scratch marks and patient says ‘there’s no scratch mark’; for thickening: Doctor asks about thickened skin and patient replies ‘no, no, I don’t think so.’
Doctor: ‘you’ve mentioned you’ve got a history of eczema’ and discussion of ‘your usual eczema’ confirms history of eczema.
Patient: ‘I, I have asthma’ directly states asthma history.
Patient: ‘usually I use a a a cream called diprobase.’
Patient: ‘in the shower I use something called dermal,’ and doctor later: ‘dermal soap,’ consistent with Dermol-type wash.

Transcript confirms OTC hydrocortisone use (‘Over the counter Hydrocortisone… you’re using the Hydrocortisone, yeah? Patient: Yes.’) but does not state it was ineffective; ineffectiveness is mentioned for antihistamines, not hydrocortisone.
Asthma meds: Doctor: ‘The blue inhaler? So you don’t use it everyday, so you just use it on and off, yeah?’ Patient: ‘Yeah. Yeah.’ This describes PRN SABA use.

Doctor: ‘You’ve tried the antihistamines and it didn’t work. OK which one did you try? Patient: The one over-the-counter. Doctor: OK, so like cetirizine, yeah?’ indicating an OTC antihistamine such as cetirizine was tried and ineffective.
Doctor: ‘So do you have any allergies to any medication at all?’ Patient: ‘No, no allergies.’
Doctor: ‘There’s no temperature… yeah? No fever?’ with no disagreement from patient, documenting absence of fever.
Doctor: ‘There’s no temperature, no joint pains, yeah?’ implies patient confirms no joint pains.
Doctor: ‘But your breathing’s all OK, yeah?’ Patient: ‘OK, yeah, yeah.’
Patient: ‘in my family, uh, there’s hypothyroidism and migraine. My mother has migraine.’
Patient: ‘hypothyroidism.’ Doctor misstates: ‘So, she has hyperthyroidism.’ The fact says hypothyroidism, which conflicts with what the doctor ultimately records.
Patient describes ‘sore and red’ skin that is ‘very itchy and, uh, dry, all over my body,’ consistent with widespread erythema and dryness reported by patient.

Patient: ‘inside of the elbows… Which is the, the worst area’ and earlier notes cracks but no weeping; also denies thickened skin and scratch marks, so worst area is antecubital fossae with cracks but no weeping, lichenification, or excoriations.

Doctor: ‘It looks like… it is quite widespread, your eczema’; patient: ‘It’s very itchy and, uh, dry’; symptoms persist despite regular emollients (Diprobase, Dermal) and concurrent OTC hydrocortisone use, indicating a widespread, pruritic, xerotic eczema flare refractory to emollients and OTC hydrocortisone.

For asthma: Doctor: ‘The blue inhaler? So you don’t use it everyday, so you just use it on and off, yeah?’ and ‘But your breathing’s all OK, yeah?’ Patient agrees, supporting intermittent, stable asthma on PRN SABA.
Doctor: ‘we’ll… you would probably need some antihistamines, which I’m going to prescribe… it’s called the antihistamine is called Fexofenadine.’

Doctor: ‘we’ll try with some Betnovate first… You, you have to use it twice a day, for the next couple of weeks’ and gives fingertip unit guidance (‘one fingertip… enough to cover your palms and your back of your hands’).
Doctor: ‘You still need to continue on your, emollients like the dermal soap, and, as well as the, diprovate. Yeah, so you still need to use those.’

Doctor: ‘If, if there’s no improvement, you need to get back to us. Or, if you have any kind of adverse reaction, like an allergic reaction… you need to get in touch with us’ and ‘If things are getting worse in the next two weeks, call us before hand. Otherwise, wait for two weeks.’
Doctor: ‘we’re going to send off the prescription to your pharmacy… it looks like Boots… so I’ll send it across to Boot’s. And it will be there for collecting.’
Asthma and blue inhaler use are discussed, but there is no explicit plan statement to ‘continue using SABA (blue inhaler) as needed’ in the management plan.
